entries.title: Global news agency AFP reports cyberattack, shuts down content platform
entries.summary: France's cybersecurity chief urges collective action to combat unprecedented threat levels in the nation.
entries.content:
France’s cybersecurity chief urges collective action to combat unprecedented threat levels in the nation.

Agence France-Presse (AFP) has been hit by a cyberattack, requiring the AFP Forum content platform to be taken offline.

The France-based international news agency’s management said on Thursday that it is currently investigating the circumstances of the cyberattack, including who was behind it.

“AFP was hit by a cyber attack overnight, starting at 1:30 am (Paris time) [00:30 GMT]. The target was AFP Forum, one of the platforms our clients use to browse and download our content,” an internal email from AFP management said.

“As soon as the intrusion was detected, our teams moved immediately to contain the intrusion and took AFP Forum offline as a precautionary measure. AFP Forum remains unavailable until further notice.”

AFP is reportedly offering backup solutions to the agency’s subscribers while the portal is offline.

France’s cybersecurity chief, Vincent Strubel, warned on Thursday that the country faces an unprecedented level of cybersecurity threats and called for collective efforts to strengthen defences against attacks.

“We are facing a level of threat that is unprecedented, with an intensity we have never experienced before,” Strubel said in an interview with France Inter radio.

The incident is the latest in a slew of cybersecurity disruptions across European countries. FIFA, which is based in Zurich, Switzerland, confirmed to Al Jazeera on Thursday that it had been the victim of a cyberattack that gave unauthorised access to personal and business information.

In October, several French supermarkets were hit by an “unprecedented” cyberattack that raised the temperature of fridges and freezers to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122F).

Temperature spikes were also recorded in stores in 10 other European countries in early November, including the United Kingdom, Germany, Belgium and Sweden.

France accused Tehran of being behind the October attack and summoned Iran’s ambassador to Paris to “lodge a very strong protest”.

Iran called Paris’s accusations “baseless” and condemned the “hackneyed policy of levelling accusations against the Islamic republic”.

entries.title: Argentina bars Central Bank from printing money to fund government spending
entries.summary: The South American country's Senate also advances proposal to suspend primary elections ahead of 2027 presidential race.
entries.content:
The South American country’s Senate also advanced a proposal to suspend primary elections ahead of the 2027 presidential race.

Argentina’s legislature has pushed forward a series of bills that would implement changes sought by President Javier Milei, including barring the Central Bank from printing extra money for government expenses.

On Thursday, the Argentinian Chamber of Deputies gave final approval to a bill imposing restrictions on the Central Bank, defining its “primary and fundamental mission” as maintaining the value of the country’s currency.

Under past administrations, the Central Bank has printed additional funds to help cover government expenses, contributing to the country’s once sky-high inflation, which reached more than 200 percent in 2023.

Milei, a libertarian economist, swept into office that year on a promise to tame runaway inflation and slash government spending.

Under his leadership, inflation has declined, though poverty has surged. Economists also believe Argentina may be drifting into a recession, with economic activity diminished in recent months.

Still, Milei’s office celebrated the Senate’s passage of the Central Bank bill with a presidential statement.

“This marks the end of nearly two decades of political manipulation at the Central Bank,” the statement said.

The bank, founded in 1935, had experienced “91 years of plunder, expropriation, impunity, and institutional decay” up to this point, it added.

The vote in the Chamber of Deputies was 141 to zero, with 99 abstentions.

The Senate previously passed the bill, though it removed language Milei had pressed for, which would have required a two-thirds vote in both chambers of Congress to remove Central Bank governors.

Bill seeks to suspend primary elections

Also on Thursday, Argentina’s Senate advanced a bill to reform the country’s elections by suspending its primaries.

Unlike the Central Bank reform, that bill was not final. It still needs to pass the Chamber of Deputies.

The bill, however, comes less than a year before Argentina is slated to hold its next presidential election. Milei is expected to seek re-election in the October 24 vote.

Critics see the suspension of primaries as a means for Milei to avoid early pushback in his campaign.

A dismal primary result, they say, could weaken his momentum ahead of the general election and cause unfavourable economic fluctuations. Milei has long faced public discontent over his programme of economic austerity.

Thursday’s bill would also reduce public financing for political parties and eliminate a mandatory presidential debate ahead of general elections.

Senators approved the legislation by a vote of 43 to 29. While members of Milei’s La Libertad Avanza party touted the bill as a means of simplifying Argentina’s elections, opponents warned it could erode democratic norms.

“Milei now wants to change the rules of democracy to improve his chances of reelection by cheating,” Buenos Aires province Governor Axel Kicillof, a potential challenger to Milei, said in a social media post.

entries.title: Georgian police clash with Turkiye’s Besiktas fans over Palestinian flag
entries.summary: Match between Besiktas and Hapoel Beer-Sheva suspended for 30 minutes after confrontation between fans and police.
entries.content:
Match between Besiktas and Hapoel Beer-Sheva suspended for 30 minutes after confrontation between fans and police in Georgia.

Georgian police have clashed with fans of Turkiye’s Besiktas after they unfurled a Palestinian flag during a Europa League game against Israel’s Hapoel Beer-Sheva.

The clashes resulted in a suspension of about 30 minutes during the 26th minute of the game held in Batumi, Georgia, but it resumed after the interruption on Thursday. Besiktas eventually won 2-1.

Turkish media outlets reported that Georgian police entered the stands and used pepper spray against fans of the Istanbul giant, prompting Danish referee Morten Krogh to stop the game with the score 0-0.

The game was relocated by UEFA to Batumi after Turkish authorities said Istanbul could not host it for safety and security reasons. Unlike two previous Hapoel away games, spectators were allowed in the stadium.

Besiktas accused Georgian police of using “disproportionate” force against supporters before and during the game.

“We strongly condemn the security forces for their use of disproportionate force against our fans,” the Turkish club said in a statement. “We also extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to all our fans affected by these incidents.”

The Turkish Football Federation also strongly condemned the treatment of Besiktas supporters, saying they were subjected to unacceptable behaviour and discrimination in a statement on X. The federation said it would press for an investigation into the incident.

Several other Turkish Super Lig clubs, including Trabzonspor, Fenerbahce, Galatasaray, Erzurumspor, Basaksehir and Samsunspor, condemned the use of force against Besiktas fans.

Prior to the match, Besiktas players refused to shake hands with their Hapoel counterparts, Turkiye’s state-run Anadolu Agency reported.

A video published by Besiktas on X after the game shows their players posing for a picture behind fans carrying a banner that reads: “Rise up against the occupation. Freedom for Palestine.”

Diplomatic incident

Turkish Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci spoke to his Georgian counterpart following the game to discuss Turkiye’s concern over the incident.

According to Turkiye’s Interior Ministry, Ciftci expressed concern over the disproportionate use of force against Turkish fans and called for measures to ensure their safe return to Turkiye.

Georgian Interior Minister Sulkhan Tamazashvili reportedly said that UEFA officials had confiscated the fans’ Palestinian flags and that Georgian state authorities had played no role in the confiscation.

entries.title: Israeli settlers damage Palestinian family’s homes in West Bank attack
entries.summary: The Tubasi family was forced out months ago and has been denied a return by settlers despite an Israeli court order.
entries.content:
The Tubasi family was forced out months ago and has been denied a return by settlers despite an Israeli court order.

Israeli settlers have smashed the foundations of two homes belonging to a Palestinian family in the occupied West Bank after attacks stopped the family from returning.

Security cameras showed the settlers bringing a bulldozer to the two-storey houses in the village of Jaloud, near Nablus, at about 1am on Thursday (23:00 GMT on Wednesday), before starting to damage them, Reuters reported. It added that the concrete foundations of the homes had been partially broken.

“This latest escalation is a direct consequence of the lack of law enforcement and the sense of impunity enjoyed by the perpetrators,” said Ghiath Nasser, the owners’ lawyer.

The Israeli military said the attack was “a serious criminal act” and said it was investigating, despite settlers remaining in the vicinity throughout the day.

A family forced out

The Tubasi family now live in a small house in Jaloud with a direct view of the homes they fled. “They want to demolish the houses so that we cannot return to them,” Wael Tubasi, one of the owners, said.

He said the deadline for the military to remove the settlers had passed.

“Even though there is a court order, and the army is required to remove them from the area entirely, not just return us to our homes, it’s still not being implemented,” he said.

The family said settlers set up a tent near their homes in April and began attacking them. They said settlers set fire to the homes, cut their water and electricity and blocked the roads.

After three months, settlers told the family they had an hour to leave or be killed “like the Dawabsheh family”, Wael’s mother, Aedah, said. In 2015, settlers set fire to the Dawabsheh family’s home in the village of Duma, killing an 18-month-old child and both his parents.

In September, soldiers escorted the family back to their homes under the court order. Ten minutes later, about 200 settlers attacked them, forcing the family and the soldiers to retreat, the family said. The settlers then burned the homes and broke much of the furniture.

“I’m forbidden from reaching my home, while the settlers have the right to remain inside. What rights are there?” Aedah said.

Surge in settler pogroms

The attack follows weeks of settler pogroms across the occupied West Bank. There have been an average of 53 settler attacks a week since the start of the year, according to the UN. The agency said on November 20 that more than 400 settler attacks causing casualties or damage had been recorded since September, more than in any previous season.

Over the weekend, settlers set fire to at least a dozen vehicles and several homes in five villages, and sprayed “Revenge” on walls. Last week, settlers killed an elderly Palestinian woman and wounded 10 other people in a pogrom near Jericho.

Very few cases lead to charges.

According to the Israeli rights group Yesh Din, 93.6 percent of investigations into settler pogroms are closed without indictments.

entries.title: In Canada, Quebec’s religious symbols ban faces a Supreme Court test
entries.summary: Canada’s top court weighs Bill 21, the Quebec law that shapes where Muslim women can work and where they feel welcome.
entries.content:
Canada’s top court weighs Bill 21, the Quebec law that shapes where Muslim women can work and where they feel welcome.

Navien Waly had been volunteering at her kids’ schools, helping out at bake sales and serving on graduation committees, for a decade when she received an email informing her that her presence was no longer welcome.

Under Quebec law, it said, parents who wore religious symbols could no longer volunteer.

Waly had started wearing the hijab four years earlier, at age 40.

She said the email felt like a “slap in the face” and that she struggled to respond when her two younger kids, who had got used to their mother’s presence at school, asked what she had done wrong.

“I’m the same person I was 10 years ago,” she said. “It doesn’t make me any different. I’ve never spoken about my religion.”

The law also upended her plans to return to work. Waly, now 45, had left a career in finance to pursue a career as a specialised educator. She was supposed to start work next year, but now, she says she can’t do the work she was trained for as long as she continues to wear the hijab.

The law behind the email, Bill 94, expanded the restrictions that Quebec first introduced under Bill 21 in 2019. On Friday, Canada’s Supreme Court is set to rule on a challenge to that earlier law, which bans public school teachers, police officers and certain other public officials from wearing religious symbols on the job.

The landmark ruling could also clarify how far governments can go in using a provision of Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms to shield laws from certain rights challenges.

‘Your livelihood or your most deeply held convictions’

In the seven years since Bill 21 passed, its impacts have been felt across religious minorities but have been particularly devastating for Muslim women.

In a survey conducted in 2022 and 2023 for a report by the National Council of Canadian Muslims (NCCM) and York University researcher Nadia Hasan, 73 percent of the 411 Muslim women surveyed said Bill 21 had impacted their job search, while 48 percent believed they didn’t get a job because of their religious identity.

Some women take their hijabs off when they get to work and put them back on when they leave, said National Council of Canadian Muslims chief executive Stephen Brown, adding that he’d spoken to women who described the routine as humiliating.

Being made to choose between “your livelihood or your most deeply held convictions”, Brown said, “was a dehumanising and cruel situation to inflict on people”.

But the consequences of the law extend beyond work. In the same survey, 88 percent of Muslim women said the law had made Quebec a less welcoming place to live.

Brown said some Muslims in Quebec had compared the climate to what they see in France, where it’s “open season on Muslims”.

Waly, who was born and raised in Canada, said in recent years, in the period coinciding with Quebec’s policies on religious symbols and her starting to wear the hijab, “things have happened to me that have never happened before”.

A couple of months ago, she was at a grocery store checkout when a man behind her started singing about how immigrants had ruined his life. He sang that he’d lost his job and been forced to retire at age 30 because of “people like you”. Waly turned around and asked in French if he was talking to her. The man went red, she recalled.

In recent years, she’s encountered more hostile looks and racist comments, with strangers telling her: “Go back to your home.”

“What home? This is my home.”

Brown said many Muslim Quebecers who speak English and who can take their work elsewhere have left the province or are planning to. For those who only speak French, relocating can be much harder, he said.

People have suggested to Waly that she move to another province, too. But she can’t imagine leaving her family and the place where she grew up. Her father, brothers, nieces and nephews all live in Quebec.

“You can’t, after living here for 45 years, to just uproot your whole life.”

How Bill 21 came to be

When Quebec introduced Bill 21 in 2019, the government presented it as a moderate approach to settling the province’s long-running debate over secularism.

The debate goes back to the 1960s Quiet Revolution when Quebec began taking control of public institutions like schools and hospitals away from the Catholic Church.

Decades later, tensions over how those institutions should accommodate religious minorities led to the Bouchard-Taylor commission. The commission recommended that judges, police and others who exercise the coercive power of the state be barred from wearing religious symbols at work.

With Bill 21, the Coalition Avenir Quebec government took things further, bringing public school teachers under the ban. Those who were already in their posts could keep wearing religious symbols as long as they didn’t change jobs or employers.

In an interview with Radio-Canada days after the law passed, Premier Francois Legault defended it, saying the majority had felt ignored on the issue for years. “To avoid extremes, you have to give a bit to the majority,” he said, suggesting the far right would want to take things even further, and stressing that religious symbols could still be worn in the street.

Polling ahead of the law passing found that 64 percent of respondents in Quebec supported the bill.

In Brown’s view, the legislation, which was put together during an election campaign, was about getting votes, tapping into longstanding distrust of organised religion, anti-Muslim sentiment and fears about the future of Quebec’s French-speaking culture.

“You combine those together, and it becomes a really effective wedge when it comes to driving support towards the party during elections,” he said.

In the years since, Quebec has expanded the restrictions beyond the jobs covered by Bill 21.

In 2025, Bill 94 extended the ban on religious symbols to school support staff and volunteers, including parents like Waly. It also required students to keep their faces uncovered at school and barred prayer on school premises.

And earlier this year, Bill 9 extended the symbols ban to include daycare staff, forbade face coverings at Quebec’s public colleges and universities, and restricted where people could pray on campus.

The newly elected Parti Quebecois government has now pledged to ban elementary school students from wearing religious symbols in schools.

What’s at stake in the Supreme Court ruling?

When Quebec passed Bill 21, it used a provision known as the notwithstanding clause, which lets governments keep a law in place even if it violates certain rights protected by Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms, including freedom of religion and the right to equality. That protection lasts up to five years at a time and can be renewed. Quebec renewed it in 2024, saying it was needed to preserve “social peace”.

A Quebec court found in 2021 that the law infringed on the rights of people who wear religious symbols, but upheld most of the law because Quebec had invoked the notwithstanding clause. The Quebec Court of Appeal upheld the ruling in 2024 and reversed an exemption for English-language school boards. The Supreme Court heard the case in March.

The NCCM, the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, the World Sikh Organization and others are challenging the law. They argue it violates constitutional rights despite Quebec’s use of the notwithstanding clause.

Brown said the council wants the court to invalidate the use of the clause in this case.

“The notwithstanding clause is supposed to be an extraordinary power of last resort,” he said, arguing it should not be used in cases where “governments are deliberately targeting the rights of citizens for political gain”.

Waly is not optimistic that the court will overturn the law, but is holding out hope that she won’t have to start over.

“At 45 years old, to start thinking of another path? I don’t know what I’m going to do,” she said. “Something’s gotta give.”

But she worries about her kids, who are now grappling with what the restrictions could mean for their future. Her oldest daughter had talked about wearing the hijab one day, but now she’s weighing it against jobs that she may want to do.

“‘Either I give up on all these different positions that I can’t do or I don’t wear the hijab,’” she recalled her daughter telling her.

“And it’s just kind of up in the air,” said Waly. “I don’t have an answer for that.”

entries.title: Report: CIA tortured more people with waterboarding than US agency admitted
entries.summary: A New York Times report lends credence to long-held belief that torture method was more widely used than acknowledged.
entries.content:
A New York Times report lends credence to the long-held belief that the torture method was more widely used than acknowledged.

The New York Times has reported that the United States Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) may have waterboarded more people than it previously admitted.

Wednesday’s report comes after the newspaper filed a lawsuit to obtain material gathered by special prosecutor John Durham, who was appointed in 2008 to investigate the CIA’s activities.

Durham’s probe ended without any criminal charges. But The New York Times obtained partially redacted documents from his investigation, including a summary of a 2012 interview with an interpreter who described a previously unconfirmed act of waterboarding.

The account sheds new light on one of the most infamous methods of torture utilised by the intelligence agency after the attacks on September 11, 2001.

Waterboarding involves restraining a person and pouring water on their face through a cloth, to mimic the experience of drowning.

The CIA called the practice an “enhanced interrogation technique”. As part of the US’s so-called “war on terror”, the agency sent suspects to overseas prisons, known as black sites, where they would be tortured in secret, including through waterboarding.

While the practice was shielded from scrutiny for years, a 2009 executive order eventually barred continued waterboarding. Congress has likewise passed restrictions.

But rights groups have long suspected that such abuses were much more widespread than the CIA admitted. The agency had previously acknowledged waterboarding three detainees.

According to the documents The New York Times received, a contract translator who worked with the CIA observed an additional case of waterboarding.

While the documents do not specify where the translator worked, the newspaper said it determined that the location was likely a black site outside of Bagram Air Force Base on the outskirts of Kabul, Afghanistan.

The translator, The New York Times explained, referenced a detainee death that matched a facility known as Detention Site Cobalt or the “Salt Pit”, which became infamous for abusive conditions.

In an interview with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the translator stated that he had seen a man referred to as “Bashir” facing the torture practice.

He described Bahir as “lying on the board with the head of the board tilted downward into the water”.

“There were approximately three to four people ‘doing this,’” the document said, summarising the translator’s statements.

The FBI summary explains that the translator “saw the incident in passing but did not participate himself”. The incident allegedly took place in a hallway.

The CIA did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment by the time of this article’s publication.

The agency has also not acknowledged waterboarding detainees at any site in Afghanistan. The three detainees it has acknowledged torturing were held at black sites in Thailand and Poland.

One was Abu Zubaydah, the first detainee the CIA held in a black-site prison, located in Thailand. The US government for years falsely depicted him as one of the highest-ranking members of al-Qaeda, a group of which he was not a member, according to US intelligence reports.

A 2014 report on the CIA torture programme by the Senate Intelligence Committee found that Zubaydah was waterboarded 83 times, sometimes as a means of helping instruct torture methods.

Another was Khalid Shaikh Mohammed, accused of being the architect of the September 11 attacks.

The third was Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri, who is accused of helping plan al-Qaeda’s 2000 bombing of a Navy destroyer, the USS Cole.

All three are currently being held in the Guantanamo Bay military prison in Cuba.

entries.title: Egypt detains driver over Cairo fuel tanker fire that killed 31
entries.summary: Prosecutors order drug tests for the 21-year-old suspect, who says he was overtaking when the crash happened.
entries.content:
Prosecutors order drug tests for the 21-year-old suspect, who says he was overtaking when the crash happened.

Prosecutors in Egypt have ordered the detention of a 21-year-old driver suspected of causing a collision on Wednesday that overturned a fuel tanker on Cairo’s ring road, starting a fire that killed 31 people.

The Public Prosecution announced on Thursday that it had ordered the man to be held pending an investigation, and sent him to the Forensic Medicine Authority for tests to determine whether he had taken drugs.

The tanker burst into flames at about 6:30pm (16:30 GMT) on Wednesday, at the height of the evening rush hour, on an elevated stretch of the ring road in al-Waraq, a densely populated district of Giza on the western edge of the capital. The fire spread to passing traffic and destroyed 27 vehicles, including cars and motorcycles.

In an earlier statement, prosecutors said the driver told investigators he had been travelling from al-Marg towards al-Haram at 110km/h (68mph), with his father in the car, and was switching lanes to overtake other vehicles when the front left of his car struck the rear right of the tanker.

The man told prosecutors he then lost control and his car veered to the far right of the road. One of the tanker’s tyres burst, the statement said, before the vehicle hit a concrete barrier and overturned. Petrol leaking from the truck caught fire.

Identifying remains

Prosecutors said they identified the driver after inspecting the scene and interviewing witnesses, and had since spoken to all the injured whose condition allowed them to be questioned. Forensic teams are taking DNA samples from victims’ relatives to identify some of the bodies. Relatives posted appeals on Facebook for men who had been on the road and had not been heard from since, the Reuters news agency reported.

The investigation will determine whether the driver bears criminal responsibility.

The Ministry of Health and Population on Thursday put the final toll at 31 dead and 26 injured, up from the 21 injured it had reported on Wednesday. Five of the injured have left hospital. The other 21 are still being treated, including eight transferred to other hospitals for further care. The bodies of the dead are in the custody of prosecutors, the ministry said.

By Thursday morning, traffic was moving again after crews cleared most of the burned wreckage. Salah Ahmed, a microbus driver, told the AP news agency that he had been on the ring road when the tanker caught fire but was held back by traffic, which saved his life.

“It was God’s hellfire on the ring road,” he said. “Why is a truck like this on the ring road at a rush hour? Who gets penalised for this happening?”

A 2018 cabinet decision barred trucks carrying more than four tonnes from the ring road between 6am and midnight, the AFP news agency reported. Prosecutors have not said why the tanker was on the road at the time.

“The tanks were exploding, the tyres were exploding, and there was fire,” Zaghlol al-Me, a local resident who reached the scene shortly after the crash, told Reuters. “We just didn’t know what to do or how to save anyone.”

Government pledges support for victims

The Public Prosecution’s statements are the first official account of how the crash happened. Early reports in local media suggested that a high-voltage cable had fallen in front of the tanker. On Wednesday night, the Ministry of Transport denied issuing any statement to that effect and said the cause was a matter for prosecutors.

The Ministry of Electricity and Renewable Energy said the overhead lines were taut when the fire began and that two circuits tripped only after it started. The ministry’s spokesman, Mansour Abdel Ghani, told the Egyptian Youm7 daily newspaper that the lines had no connection to the crash and melted in the heat. A high-voltage line lay twisted on the ground on Thursday, AP reported.

President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi ordered full medical care for the injured and support for the families of those killed. Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly visited the injured on Thursday with Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar and Social Solidarity Minister Maya Morsy. Madbouly said the government, civil society and businesspeople would provide bank investment certificates to give bereaved families a stable income, and replacement vehicles for people whose cars burned.

“We realise that no compensation or money can make up for those we have lost,” Madbouly said.

Egypt’s Ministry of Social Solidarity said on Thursday that people could donate through the InstaPay app to help the injured and the families of those killed. It also opened an account at Nasser Social Bank for donations from businesses and civil society groups. The cabinet said the ministry had received 24 million Egyptian pounds (about $445,000) from seven charities.

Calls for accountability

The crash has renewed questions about road safety in Egypt. The Ministry of Transport says it spent about $37bn on transport between 2014 and 2024, yet 5,829 people were killed on the country’s roads in 2025, up 10.8 percent from the year before, and about 84,000 were injured, according to the state statistics agency, CAPMAS.

Egyptian legislators demanded accountability on Thursday. Mahmoud Samy, an MP, said the government needed to move from “building roads and expanding them to managing their safety professionally”. Abdel Moneim Imam, a politician who chairs the liberal Justice Party, said the cabinet bore full responsibility and should resign.

Amr Moussa, Egypt’s former foreign minister and former secretary-general of the Arab League, also criticised what he described as a deterioration in government oversight.

“Trading accusations and evading responsibility leads to the next disaster,” Moussa said, according to Reuters.

Transport Minister Kamel al-Wazir was appointed in 2019 after a train crash at Cairo’s Ramses station triggered a fire that killed 25 people, according to Reuters. He has rejected calls to resign since then, including after a lorry crash in the Nile Delta that killed 19 people, almost all of them young women, last year. The ministry declined to comment further when contacted by Reuters.

Earlier this month, a train crash, also in Giza, killed at least seven people and injured more than 125, prompting calls from legislators for accountability over recurring transport accidents.
